title: One game designer directing a team of AI agents: what it took to ship a 90s-style RTS that runs in the browser
author: LastingDynamicsGames
selftext:
I run a small software company and started this as an experiment: can one person, directing AI agents, build and ship a complete real-time strategy campaign in the spirit of the 90s games I grew up with? It turned into Forgotten Dynasty: 5 stories, 10 houses, 15 missions, HTML5 Canvas, playable in the browser on desktop, tablet and phone.

How the work is split:

\- Engine: a deterministic simulation in plain JavaScript (pathfinding, AI opponents, missions), with headless tests that replay the five stories and check the results are identical run after run. Agents write the code, the tests decide if it lands.

\- Units and animations: AI-generated pixel art (PixelLab and image models), sometimes from a 3D model first, then scripts that check every frame at game scale: direction, contact with the ground, size against the other units. The trick that changed everything was writing down every mistake I caught in playtesting as a rule the agents re-read before drawing the next creature. Now most units pass in one or two rounds.

\- Music: composed by an agent as MIDI and rendered with free SoundFonts, so every track has an editable source and a clear licence.

\- Me: direction, playtesting every mission, and saying no a lot.

What AI is still bad at: consistency across eight walking directions, and anything it cannot "see" at real size. Units walking backwards in the tutorial was a real bug last month.

Story I is free and plays as a guest, no signup. Stories II–V are a one-time €9.99:

[https://forgottendynasty.com/play?utm\_source=reddit&utm\_medium=post&utm\_campaign=aigamedev](https://forgottendynasty.com/play?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=aigamedev)

Happy to go deeper on any part of the pipeline. What's the hardest thing you've had to keep consistent across AI-generated assets?
